Cupidity

/kyoo-PID-ih-tee/ - the stress falls on PID · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Cupidity means an overpowering greed for wealth.

The board meeting turned tense when the founder proposed cutting safety inspections to widen profits - cupidity dressed up as efficiency, one engineer muttered.

Worked Example

The lottery winner's cousin appeared within a week, full of investment ideas that all happened to route the money through his own accounts. When the winner hesitated, the cousin dropped the pretense and simply demanded a share. It was cupidity in its plainest form: not need, not a plan to build anything, just hunger for someone else's money.

Cupidity is narrower and harsher than greed: it is greed aimed specifically at wealth, and it carries the writer's judgment that the craving has taken the person over. A dragon coiled on a pile of gold is the picture cupidity paints.

How Cupidity Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

greed

greed: wanting too much of anything - food, power, money - not just wealth

covetousness

covetousness: fixated wanting of what belongs to someone else

acquisitiveness

acquisitiveness: the collector's itch to obtain, milder and more neutral

Antonyms

generosity

generosity: open-handed giving

contentment

contentment: satisfaction with what one already has

How Strong Is It? — longing → greed → cupidity

longing vs. cupidity

longing vs. cupidity: Longing is any strong wish and can be perfectly innocent; there is nothing innocent about cupidity.

greed vs. cupidity

greed vs. cupidity: Greed is the broad vice of wanting too much of anything; cupidity sharpens it into an overpowering hunger for wealth in particular.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of cupidity.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — cupid-

Root — cupid-: full of desire (Latin cupidus, from cupere, to desire)

Suffix — -ity

Suffix — -ity: state of being

Put it together

Put it together: Cupid- (Latin cupidus, 'full of desire,' from cupere, 'to desire') + -ity (the state of being) = the state of being full of desire. Latin cupiditas could name any burning desire; English kept only the darkest slice - desire for money. There is nothing else to peel off here: the root survives in no other everyday English word, though the Romans personified desire itself as the winged god Cupido.

The god behind the greed

The god behind the greed: Latin cupere, 'to desire,' lives on in English only inside this word - and in a name you already know: Cupid, the winged Roman god of desire who still shows up every February. Cupidity is that desire gone hard and hungry for gold.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Cupidity is a courtroom-and-editorial word: it accuses. Everyday speech says greed. Reach for cupidity when the greed is specifically for money and you want the sentence to pass judgment - and note that despite the shared god, it has nothing to do with modern valentine romance.
